		<h2 class="research-title">Embodied complexity</h2>
		<div class="research-lede">
		  <h3><i>Can we experience complexity, rather than merely observe it?</i></h3>
		</div>
	</section>


	<section class="research-subpage-section">
		<h2 class="research-section-title">Overview</h2>
		<p>
		  Complex systems are often introduced through equations, simulations, and abstract models. While these are indispensable scientific tools, they can sometimes obscure the intuitive experience of <a href="../resources/glossary.html#emergence">emergence</a> itself. I am interested in designing interactive systems that allow people to participate in complexity — not simply by watching patterns unfold, but by becoming part of the dynamics that generate them and using their own sensory apparatus.
		</p>

		<p>
		  My work in embodied complexity explores how ideas from <a href="../resources/glossary.html#cybernetics">cybernetics</a>, <a href="../resources/glossary.html#complexity-science">complexity science</a>, and <a href="../resources/glossary.html#self-organisation">self-organisation</a> can be experienced through physical interaction, collaborative activities, and creative media. Rather than treating participants as passive observers, these projects invite them to become interacting agents whose local decisions collectively shape global outcomes.
		</p>
		<p>
		  Current projects include <strong>Musical Allostasis</strong>, an interactive framework in which participants create a collective soundscape through local listening, anticipation and <a href="../resources/glossary.html#adaptation">adaptation</a>, together with a growing collection of online demonstrations that explore pattern formation, emergence, and adaptive systems. Through these activities, I hope to make complex systems more tangible, accessible, and enjoyable while opening new opportunities for research, education, and public engagement.
		</p>
	</section>
